messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 47
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Ministry Worker
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 59

**Vignette: Elena, Age 47**

Elena has spent the better part of two decades working with vulnerable women in her community — survivors of domestic violence, trafficking, and poverty. She knows how to sit with other people's pain. What she has never quite learned is how to sit with her own.

Three years ago, Elena was sexually assaulted by a colleague — a man she had known for years, someone who shared her office, her mission, her faith. She had stayed late one evening to finish grant paperwork, and he had stayed too. She does not talk about what happened in detail. What she will say is that she drove home afterward, washed her clothes, and went to bed beside her husband without saying a word. She told herself she would deal with it later. Later has not come.

In the weeks after the assault, Elena threw herself into her work with an intensity that alarmed her supervisor. She was at the office before anyone else arrived and left after everyone had gone. She told herself she was needed. The women she served were in real danger — what had happened to her, she reasoned, was not something she had the right to fall apart over. She had seen worse. She had held the hands of women who had survived worse.

But her body refused to cooperate with this logic. She began having nightmares so vivid and physical that she would wake up choking, convinced someone was in the room. Her husband, Rodrigo, would reach for her in the dark and she would recoil from his touch before she was fully awake, then spend the rest of the night rigid with shame. Their marriage, once easy and affectionate, has become a careful, quiet distance that neither of them fully names.

At work, Elena can no longer attend the support groups she used to facilitate for assault survivors. She has handed those off to a younger colleague, citing administrative responsibilities. The truth is that sitting in that circle — listening to women describe what was done to them — sends her into a state she can only describe as disappearing. Her vision narrows. Her chest locks. She has learned to excuse herself before it becomes visible.

She is hypervigilant in ways that exhaust her. She parks in a different spot every day. She checks the office locks three times before leaving. When a male colleague lingers in a doorway, her body floods with adrenaline and she has to remind herself, slowly and deliberately, where she is. The man who assaulted her no longer works at the organization — he resigned quietly, months later, for reasons officially unrelated — but his absence has not made the building feel safe.

Elena has not told Rodrigo what happened. She has constructed a version of herself that functions, that makes dinner, that asks about his day. She is a skilled listener by profession, and she has turned that skill inward in the worst possible way — monitoring herself constantly for signs that she is becoming someone her family cannot recognize. She worries she is already there.

What brings her in now, three years later, is not a crisis but an accumulation. Last month, a young woman came into the ministry office and described her assault in language so precise and familiar that Elena had to leave the room. She sat in the bathroom for twenty minutes, shaking, before she could return. That evening, she looked up a therapist's number. She waited two weeks to call. When she finally did, she told the receptionist she was calling on behalf of a client.

She corrects herself at the first session, quietly, without elaborating. She is a woman who has spent her life advocating for others to seek help. She is still learning, at forty-seven, that the invitation was always meant for her too.
